assumptions: A narrowly selected buyer segment has recurring evidence obligations not adequately met by its existing GRC or MLOps tools.
Customers will authorize development-system connectors after appropriate security controls are established.
Initial gap assessments can be delivered without relying on confidential employer resources.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Signed paid assessments from a sharply defined high-risk segment, proof of conversion to prepaid workspaces, measured audit-preparation savings, connector authorization, retention across model changes, and partner-sourced acquisition economics.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Continuous evidence captured inside development workflows is structurally better than reconstructing regulated AI documentation periodically.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: High-risk providers and deployers face consequential evidence work, but system classification, near-term urgency, and preference for standalone software are unknown.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Prepaid recurring workspaces could deliver strong margins and retention as evidence accumulates, but connector upkeep, security, specialist review, CAC, and the projected 500 accounts are unproven.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: CEE AI providers using a selected MLOps stack could form a coherent beachhead, yet the number of qualifying high-risk systems may be limited and fragmented.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: A focused CEE product could establish expertise, but cloud, MLOps, GRC, and consulting incumbents control adjacent workflows and can add equivalent features.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: The evidence layer can extend across systems, standards, procurement reviews, model risk, vendors, and EU geographies if integrations gain adoption.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Accumulated mappings and workflow history can create switching costs, but the business currently controls neither integrations nor exclusive data and remains replaceable.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Automated continuous capture could materially reduce audit preparation, though that improvement has not been measured and bundled governance suites may match it.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Staged AI Act application creates increasing evidence needs, but extended or simplified high-risk timelines can defer purchases.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Auditors, law firms, and development agencies are plausible trust channels, but all are prospective and enterprise compliance sales lack validation.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: Founder-product fit and a service-led MVP are favorable, while legal accuracy, security expectations, heterogeneous integrations, and part-time enterprise selling are substantial.

highest_value_structural_change: Narrow the beachhead to one regulated AI category and one dominant development stack, then secure an auditor-backed evidence standard and distribution partnership.
main_structural_strength: Evidence naturally accumulates across model changes, giving a well-integrated product recurring utility and potential switching costs.
primary_score_limiter: The target systems, workflow access, standalone-product demand, and distribution partnerships are all unvalidated while powerful adjacent vendors can bundle the feature.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Many AI systems will not be high-risk and can use generic document or existing governance tools, while regulatory delays can postpone urgency.
